one_liner: C parser and emitter for UCL, an nginx-style JSON superset; README shows it parsing JSON about 2x faster than jansson.
what_it_does: Parses UCL configuration files (nginx-like syntax, comments, macros, .include with priorities and merge policies, variables, heredoc strings, number and time suffixes) and plain JSON, MessagePack, CBOR and canonical S-expressions into a reference-counted ucl_object_t tree, and emits that tree as UCL config, JSON, compact JSON, YAML (limited), MessagePack or CBOR. It also validates objects against JSON Schema draft v4. The API is its own (ucl_parser_new, ucl_parser_add_chunk or add_file, ucl_parser_get_object, ucl_object_lookup, ucl_object_emit) plus a C++ wrapper in ucl++.h and Lua bindings, so it does not drop in for jansson's json_t API.
how_it_is_fast: A hand-written single-pass state-machine parser classifies each byte through a 256-entry character-class bitmask table (ucl_chartable.h) instead of chains of comparisons. With UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY, keys and values that need no unescaping, lowercasing or variable expansion point into the input buffer instead of being malloc'd and copied, which cuts allocation on string-heavy JSON. Object members sit in klib khash tables keyed with mum-hash (since 0.7.0; the README numbers predate this and used uthash). There is no SIMD; it is a byte-at-a-time scanner that also tracks line and column numbers.
when_to_use: C or C++ daemons that want a human-friendly config format with includes, priorities, macros and comments that still accepts plain JSON
Reading admin-controlled configuration and converting it to JSON, MessagePack or CBOR in one library
Config files of kilobytes to a few megabytes where 30-60 MB/s parse speed is far more than enough
You need JSON Schema v4 validation of the loaded config without a second library
Platforms where FreeBSD-style tooling is expected: FreeBSD builds it in base as a private library
when_not_to_use: Bulk or hot-path JSON parsing: its own best figure is about 63 MB/s (-O3, derived from page data), measured in 2013 against jansson only, so a dedicated JSON parser is the better starting point

Untrusted or adversarial input: the README says it is for trusted inputs only, and the open issue list carries many fuzzer-found memory-safety reports (use-after-free in ucl_hash_sort #388 and .inherit #387, possible heap overflow in macro parsing #367, OOB read #407, NULL dereference #410)
Reading YAML, TOML or XML: YAML is write-only and limited, TOML and XML are not supported
You need strict JSON semantics: duplicate keys silently become implicit arrays, relaxed syntax is accepted, and MessagePack or CBOR output keeps only the first value of an implicit array
Multi-threaded parsing of untrusted keys: the hash seed defaults to time(NULL) and is lazily set through an unsynchronized static

integration.dependencies: none required; optional libcurl or libfetch (URL includes), OpenSSL (signed includes), POSIX regex.h (schema patterns, on by default in autotools), Lua or LuaJIT (bindings)
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler (no -std pinned in the CMake or autotools files); C++11 for the ucl++.h wrapper; CMake or autotools
integration.platforms: any; Linux, BSDs and macOS are the main targets, Windows builds exist (_WIN32 code paths, POSIX-only tests skipped since 0.9.4)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; parsers are per-instance, but the mum-hash seed is a lazily initialised static with no synchronization, so create the first parser before starting threads

gotchas: UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY requires the input buffer to outlive every object, and zero-copy strings are not NUL-terminated; open issue #352 (Feb 2026, PR #353 open) reports a use-after-free when ZEROCOPY is combined with ucl_parser_add_file* because the library unmaps its own buffer, and #323 a SEGV emitting zero-copy keys with embedded NUL bytes.

Hash seeding is time(NULL) unless the embedder defines UCL_RANDOM_FUNCTION at build time, so key-collision flooding is predictable; UCL_PARSER_SAFE_FLAGS plus ucl_parser_set_limits() are the documented hardening for less-trusted input, and only max_depth (1024) is limited by default.

The README benchmark is a single run per figure that has been unchanged since tag 0.2.0 (2013-12-03), before the 0.7.0 move from uthash to klib; tests/speed.test pre-reads the file into page cache ('Preread file to cheat benchmark!'), test_speed.c starts the timer after mmap and parses with ZEROCOPY, and the jansson harness, version and build flags were never published, so the 2.1x parse ratio compares an unknown jansson build against a zero-copy UCL parse.
Emitting returns a malloc'd buffer per call (free it), and the two README UCL result sets differ in optimisation level, so the -O3 figures cannot be set against the jansson numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (rapidyaml, libfyaml, fkYAML, toml++ challengers such as teptris and TOMLDecoder, pugixml-class XML parsers) parse YAML, TOML or XML, which libucl cannot read; pick libucl only when you control the config format and want nginx-style UCL with includes, priorities and JSON/MessagePack/CBOR interchange in one C library, and use rapidyaml or libfyaml for YAML input and a TOML or XML sibling for those formats.
verified_claims_summary: The README times one parse of a generated JSON file of about 19 MB and 700 thousand lines (it matches the repo's tests/rcl_test.json.xz, which decompresses to 19,001,364 bytes and 693,050 lines): UCL 0.6649 s versus jansson 1.3899 s, about 2.1x or roughly 28.6 versus 13.7 MB/s (derived from page data), and 0.3002 s (about 63 MB/s) with UCL rebuilt at -O3; JSON emit is 0.2329 s versus 0.2609 s (about 1.1x). No CPU, compiler, jansson version or flags are given, the jansson harness is not public, and the numbers date from no later than December 2013.
status_note: Actively maintained (0.9.4 released 2026-02-17, commits and new issue reports into October 2026), BSD-2-Clause and copyable, and built in FreeBSD base as a private library, but the open fuzzer-found memory-safety issues mean it should only see trusted configuration input.
